notes:
What's new in 0.3.1:

- Faster, more accurate transcription. Dicta now runs a newer version of its Parakeet speech engine, which made roughly a quarter fewer mistakes than 0.3.0 on our recorded test dictations. On NVIDIA PCs it downloads an updated GPU pack by itself (about 1.7 GB, once) and a sharper version of the model (about 1.1 GB, once), then transcribes on the graphics card, usually in a fraction of a second. On other PCs it keeps running on the CPU with nothing to set up.
- A GPU driver crash can no longer take Dicta down. Transcription on the graphics card now runs in a separate helper process. If the driver ever crashes mid-dictation, Dicta retries that dictation on the CPU and keeps your words; after repeated crashes it stays on the CPU until the next restart.
- Full rewrite keeps what you actually said. It no longer deletes words you repeat on purpose ("no, no, no") or side comments, and it handles spoken lists properly: "first … second … third" or "my to-do list number one … number two …" become a numbered list without losing the lead-in or any words in the items. If the rewrite would drop words, Dicta falls back to plain cleanup, which now also formats the list and removes "um" and "uh" while keeping real words such as "ER" and "uh-huh".
- Numbers stay intact. Codes spoken digit by digit ("seven, seven, four") come out as 774, and Light cleanup no longer splits "1,000" or "3:30" apart.
- Pasting works from more apps, and your clipboard comes back. Copies from Notepad, Chrome and other apps that use richer clipboard formats used to make Dicta type your words letter by letter; they now paste normally, and whatever you had copied, including images, is restored afterwards. When Dicta does have to type, the letters no longer arrive garbled.
- Learning is safer. If its saved data is ever damaged or too large, Dicta pauses learning, keeps the original file, and tells you, instead of retrying forever.
